dialogs.title: Dialog — Bij de Albert Heijn
dialogs.intro: The supermarket, late afternoon. Budi is looking for one ingredient he assumes this country won't have.

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.id: Aisle seven, next to the pasta.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En hebben jullie ook kecap manis?
lines.id: And do you have kecap manis too?
lines.literal: and have you(pl) also ketjap manis?

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.id: Sure. In the world foods section, bottom shelf.

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.text: Natuurlijk. We eten hier veel Indonesisch.
lines.id: Of course. We eat a lot of Indonesian food here.
lines.literal: naturally. we eat here much Indonesian.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dat wist ik niet. Mag ik ook een half pond kaas?
lines.id: I didn't know that. Could I also have half a pound of cheese?
lines.literal: that knew I not. may I also a half pound cheese?

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.text: Bij de kaasafdeling. Wilt u jong of oud?
lines.id: At the cheese counter. Young or old?
lines.literal: at the cheese-counter. want you young or old?

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.text: Oude kaas is droger en veel scherper.
lines.id: Old cheese is drier and much sharper.
lines.literal: old cheese is drier and much sharper.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dan neem ik een paar plakjes oude kaas.
lines.id: Then I'll take a few slices of old cheese.
lines.literal: then take I a pair slice-lets old cheese.

lines.speaker: Medewerker:
lines.text: Prima. Verder nog iets? Anders: kassa vier is vrij.
lines.id: Fine. Anything else? If not: checkout four is free.
lines.literal: good. further still something? otherwise: checkout four is free.

notes: **Waar staat de rijst?** — Dutch picks its verb by the object's shape: *staan* (stand) for upright things, *liggen* (lie) for flat things, *zitten* (sit) for things inside something. *De melk staat in de koelkast*, *het boek ligt op tafel*.
**Onderin** = at the bottom (of a shelf). Its family: *bovenin*, *achterin*, *voorin*, *middenin*.

**We eten hier veel Indonesisch** — and that's true. Indonesian dishes are part of everyday Dutch food, a legacy of colonial history: *nasi*, *bami*, *saté*, *kroepoek*, *sambal*, and *ketjap* are in almost every supermarket. The words came into Dutch whole, sometimes with surprising spellings.
**Dat wist ik niet** — the past tense of *weten*. The past isn't covered until unit 17, but this sentence is too useful to put off.

**Jong of oud?** — a cheese's age decides its taste: *jong* (4 weeks, mild), *belegen* (4 months), *oud* (10 months, sharp with salt crystals), *overjarig* (over a year). You'll be asked this every time you buy cheese in the Netherlands.
**Een paar plakjes** — *een paar* means "a few", not "a pair" (it can mean that too, when the context is clear: *een paar schoenen*). *Plakje* = a thin slice, the diminutive of *plak*.
**Kassa vier is vrij** — *vrij* means free/available. In Dutch supermarkets you bag your own groceries: plastic bags cost money and nobody packs for you. Bring your own *boodschappentas*.

grammars.title: Vague amounts
body: Where English juggles "some", "a few", and "a little", Dutch also sorts its words by the kind of noun.
after: *Veel* and *weinig* work for both countable and uncountable nouns — a freedom English doesn't have (*many/much*, *few/little*).
⚠️ *Wat* leads two lives: the question word "what" and the amount word "some". Its position decides: *Wat wil je?* versus *Ik wil wat water.*
*Nog wat* = a bit more: *Wil je nog wat koffie?*

grammars.title: Measures and packaging
body: After a measure word, the noun stands **with no article and no *van***: *een kilo appels*, not *een kilo van de appels* — unlike English "a kilo of apples".

Meaning
Example
rows: een pak melk, een pak rijst

after: ⚠️ *Een ons* = 100 grams, not an English ounce (28 g). Ordering *twee ons* at the cheese shop gets you 200 grams — the measure the Dutch use most.
Measure words don't take a plural after a number: *drie kilo*, *twee ons*, *vijf liter* — not *drie kilo's*.

blocks.title: Dutch supermarkets: good to know
items: **Albert Heijn** (the biggest), **Jumbo**, **Lidl**, **Aldi**, and the **toko** (Asian grocery) for a full range of Asian ingredients.
*Bonuskaart* / *bonus* — the store's discount card. Without it, you pay full price for items on promotion.
Shopping bags **cost extra** and aren't handed out automatically. *Wilt u een tasje?* — say yes, and you pay for it.
*Statiegeld* — the deposit: return bottles and cans to a machine; the receipt is deducted from your total.
Saturday afternoon and Sunday can be very busy; many small shops close on Sunday and Monday morning.
⚠️ Most supermarkets **accept only debit cards** — recall unit 6.

blocks.text: *Houdbaar tot* (use by) and *ten minste houdbaar tot* (best before) are printed on every package — two phrases worth learning before your first shop.

For Asian ingredients, the key word is *toko* — borrowed from Indonesian, where it simply means "shop", but in Dutch it specifically means an Asian grocery. *Is er een toko in de buurt?* will be understood at once.
